newsitem.title: FRANCE: Little impact seen in French civil service strike.
newsitem.headline: Little impact seen in French civil service strike.

text.p: French civil servants go on strike over wage demands on Thursday but the impact of their protest will be blunted as public transport is not involved.
The 24-hour stoppage comes against a background of social unrest as the centre-right government enforces budget austerity to comply with the criteria to join the European single currency in 1999.
Seven trade unions have called on the country's four million public employees to stop work, saying the government wage offer for this year and next will cut their purchasing power.
Demonstrations and rallies are expected to jam traffic in cities and many schools will be closed, but the protest is not expected to cause major disruption to the public.

Public transport workers are holding separate wage talks and will not join the protest. Staff at SNCF state railways staged their own strike last month, and public transport workers in many cities have reached deals on pay and working hours after protracted strikes over the past month.
Thursday's protest should mostly affect state schools and hospitals where unions also complain about budget restraint and job cuts, as well as postal services.
The strike by tax inspectors will even be welcome for taxpayers: the finance ministry has put off to next Monday from Thursday the deadline for sending in tax returns.
Automation of services at France Telecom and utilities Electricite de France and Gaz de France mean the stoppage will have little consequences on consumers.
The trade unions threw down the gauntlet after turning down a government offer of a 2.8 percent pay rise for 1997 and 1998 which they said will not compensate for a 1996 pay freeze.
They say wages are due to increase by one percent through 1996 and 1997 while prices are forecast to rise 3.6 percent.

Civil Service Minister Dominique Perben disputed the figures in an interview in Wednesday's tabloid Le Parisien, saying civil service wages would increase by 2.6 percent on average this year taking into account promotions.
"This is a satisfactory figure compared with an expected prise rise of 1.3 percent and the general evolution of salaries in the country," he said.
Perben said civil servants were not losing in the long run as their wages had increased by nearly 30 percent over the past six years while prices rose 16 percent.

He has rejected a "catch-up" for last year, saying it would cost 20 billion francs ($3.5 billion) and the government was determined to show its European Union partners and financial markets it would stick firmly to budget restraint.
The strike has raised little sympathy among the public who highly value the civil service's job security at a time of acute unemployment.

A BVA opinion poll said 56 percent of 924 voters questioned favoured the civil servants' job security being called into question if their wages were raised significantly, to 38 percent who opposed it.

In a separate conflict, unions at privatised carmaker Renault have called a one-hour strike on Friday at all plants in France, Belgium and Spain to protest at the shutfown of the Vilvoorde plant in Belgium and other planned job cuts.
